title: There will never be a theory of everything
subtitle: Donald Hoffman responds to his critics
author: Donald Hoffman
introduction: In his book,The Case Against Reality, Donald Hoffman used evolutionary theory to argue that we don’t see reality as it truly is. Perception evolved to construct useful fictions, not to access truth. Hoffman’s critics claim that his argument is self-defeating, since evolutionary theory is itself based on supposedly true perceptions of organisms and their reproductive processes. In this article, Hoffman responds. His critics, he argues, misunderstand the nature of scientific theories, which are never the final word, but are rather provisional models, destined to sow the seeds of their own replacement by deeper theories.
body:
We can capture images of black holes, cure many diseases, send spaceships beyond our solar system, and build technologies with capabilities that, to our forbears, would be indistinguishable from magic. Science has been wildly successful. Scientific theories have dramatically evolved in their sophistication and technological promise. Is science on the verge of completing its mission to discover the Theory of Everything? Should we encourage bright students to go elsewhere?

The very nature of scientific theories and their evolution ensures that there can never be a final Theory of Everything.

I think that there is, in principle, infinite job security in science. The very nature of scientific theories and their evolution ensures that there can never be a final Theory of Everything. Bright students can feel secure. Here’s why.

A scientific theory proposes assumptions and offers explanations.

Einstein’s special theory of relativity, for instance, proposed the assumption of relativity: the laws of physics are the same in all inertial reference frames. And it proposed constancy: light moves at the same speed in a vacuum for all inertial observers, regardless of their motion.

SUGGESTED VIEWING Truth, theory and ultimate reality With Abby Innes, Bernard Carr, Lisa Randall, Tim Maudlin

Given these assumptions, his theory explains why moving clocks tick more slowly, why moving objects appear shorter, and why mass and energy are interchangeable.

Or consider evolution by natural selection. It assumes a population of interacting organisms that replicate. Each reproduces in proportion to its fitness, which depends on its genetic or cultural strategies, and how they interact with the strategies of other organisms. Replication, inheritance, and occasional mutations allow strategies to spread at varying rates through the population.

These assumptions are made precise in the mathematics of evolutionary game theory. It explains many biological phenomena, including a remarkable variety of surprising behaviours.

For instance, jewel beetles in the outback of Western Australia are dimpled, glossy, and brown. Females are flightless. Males fly about looking for an available female. If, however, a male spots a beer bottle that is dimpled, glossy, and brown, it alights and endlessly caresses the bottle, seeking in vain to mate.

This is perhaps surprising. After all, male beetles have successfully reproduced for thousands of years. Surely, we might suppose, evolution shaped their senses to truly know their females. They shouldn’t be fooled by an inanimate object much larger than real females.

This alluring bottle is just one example of a supernormal stimulus. Nature has many more.

For instance, many insects, particularly certain species of dragonflies, mayflies, midges, and water beetles, use polarized light as a cue to locate bodies of water where they can lay their eggs. They find oil slicks, asphalt, and other highly polarizing surfaces irresistible, even though they are death traps.

For humans, supernormal stimuli often underlie attractions to junk food, cosmetics, pornography, video games, horror movies, gambling, and ASMR. Many advertisements cleverly use supernormal stimuli to catch attention and hold interest.

In short, sensory systems evolved to help us have kids, not to show us the truth.

Evolutionary game theory offers a compelling explanation for supernormal stimuli. Evolution by natural selection shapes the sensory systems of organisms to respond to cues that historically increased survival and reproduction. However, these adaptations are based on past environments, not on an absolute understanding of present reality. Because selection favors strong responses to reliable cues, organisms develop sensory biases –preferences for exaggerated versions of beneficial stimuli. When an environment changes (perhaps, in some cases, due to human influence), these biases can be exploited by artificially intensified stimuli, leading to supernormal responses. So supernormal stimuli arise when evolutionary shortcuts – once adaptive – are amplified beyond their original purpose, leading to overreactions in new contexts.

In short, sensory systems evolved to help us have kids, not to show us the truth. Male jewel beetles evolved not to know the truth about females, but simply to look for something dimpled, glossy, and brown – the bigger the better.

Indeed, one can use the mathematics of evolutionary game theory to prove that the probability is zero that any sensory system reports the truth about any of a wide variety of structures that reality might have.

This is stunning, because it entails that our perceptions of tables and chairs, forks and spoons, and all other physical objects in space and time, no more accurately represent reality than does the jewel beetle’s representation of a female. Evolution did not shape our senses to be a window on reality. Instead, our senses are like a simplified user interface that lets us play the game of life, much as your desktop interface lets you successfully interact with the complexity of the diodes, resistors, and voltages in your computer. Seeing the truth gets in the way. If you had to toggle voltages to write an email, your friends might never hear from you.

But wait, haven’t we just gotten ourselves in a logical bind? Evolution starts by assuming there are physical objects in space and time, such as organisms and resources. But when we formalize evolution using evolutionary games, we conclude that our perception of physical objects is not the truth, just an adaptive fiction. We assume physical objects, and then conclude that they can’t be real. Isn’t this a self-defeating way of arguing?

SUGGESTED VIEWING After Darwin With Massimo Pigliucci, Tim Lewens, David Malone, Zanna Clay

We could put the problem like this. Either evolutionary game theory properly models biological evolution or it does not. If it does not, then whatever it says about the basic assumptions of evolution can’t be taken seriously. And if it does, then it couldn’t possibly contradict the basic assumptions of evolution. In either case, we can dismiss the radical conclusion that our perception of physical objects is a fiction.

Some philosophers use this sort of argument to try to recover the idea that we evolved to see reality as it really is. But this is misguided. It entirely misunderstands the nature and evolution of scientific theories. It is straightforward to see why.

A scientific theory proposes assumptions and offers explanations. It does not explain its assumptions. It assumes them. In this sense, the assumptions of a scientific theory are the explicit “miracles” of that theory. The theory says, “If you grant me these assumptions, then I can explain all this other wonderful stuff.”

In Einstein’s special relativity, light is assumed, not explained. That the speed of light is the same for all inertial observers is also assumed, not explained. These are big miracles. If you want a scientific explanation of them, then you need a deeper theory. Indeed, 46 years after Einstein published special relativity, he wrote a letter to his friend Michele Besso, admitting “All these fifty years of conscious brooding have brought me no nearer to the answer to the question ‘What are light quanta?’ Nowadays every Tom, Dick, and Harry thinks they know it, but they are mistaken.” Einstein still wanted a theory that explained key assumptions of special relativity.

Every scientific theory starts with unexplained assumptions. Therefore, every scientific theory has hard limits to its scope of explanations. At a minimum, its scope excludes its assumptions, but it may exclude much more. Thus there is not now, and never will be, a scientific theory of everything. This is great news. That’s the reason there is, at least in principle, infinite job security in science.

Notice that this argument for limited scope does not depend on the kind of explanation offered by the theory. It doesn’t matter if the explanations are, for instance, inductive, statistical, deductive-nomological, causal-mechanical, unificationist, pragmatic, or contextual. In each case, the scope is limited.

This is science at its best: a scientific theory telling us the limits of its own foundational concepts, and thereby urging us to seek a deeper theory. This is not the logical equivalent of shooting oneself in the foot.

How do we find the necessary limits of a scientific theory? Good scientific theories give us mathematical tools to explore their scope. Great scientific theories give us, in addition, mathematical tools to find their limits. For instance, Einstein’s special and general theories of relativity, together with quantum field theory, entail that spacetime itself has hard limits: spacetime has no operational meaning beyond the Planck scale, roughly 10⁻³³ centimetres and 10⁻⁴³ seconds. These theories tell us that their key foundational assumption, spacetime itself, must be replaced by something deeper. In consequence, many high-energy theoretical physicists are looking for new foundations beyond spacetime, and are finding fascinating new vistas such as amplituhedra, associahedra, and surfaceology.

This is science at its best: a scientific theory telling us the limits of its own foundational concepts, and thereby urging us to seek a deeper theory. This is not the logical equivalent of shooting oneself in the foot. Rather, it is one of the greatest gifts of the scientific method: an antidote to dogmatism and complacency.

The antidote is absolutely needed to counter human nature. Proponents of a scientific theory easily fall into the trap of believing that their theory, and its foundational concepts, are the final word, with just a little mopping up left to do.

In 1894, for instance, Albert Michelson of the famous Michelson-Morley experiment on light argued that “The more important fundamental laws and facts of physical science have all been discovered, and these are now so firmly established that the possibility of their ever being supplanted in consequence of new discoveries is exceedingly remote. [...] Our future discoveries must be looked for in the sixth place of decimals.” In his lifetime, relativity and quantum theory proved him wrong.

This feature of human nature prompted Max Planck to suggest that science advances one funeral at a time: “A new scientific truth does not triumph by convincing its opponents and making them see the light, but rather because its opponents eventually die, and a new generation grows up that is familiar with it.”

SUGGESTED VIEWING Turtles all the way down With Priyamvada Natarajan, Hilary Lawson, Jack Symes, Donald Hoffman

Modern evolutionary theory is impressive. It provides unprecedented insight into biological systems and their interactions, and into human psychology and its foibles. It has, at present, no serious contenders, no theory rivalling its explanatory scope.

But, like all scientific theories, evolution has limited scope and must eventually be replaced by a deeper theory. Impressively, it gives us tools to find its limits. And the limits it reveals agree with those revealed by physics: spacetime and its objects cannot be fundamental.

Finding such limits is not shooting ourselves in the foot, but almost like pulling ourselves up by our bootstraps. Almost, but not quite. A scientific theory may tell us its limits, but it cannot tell us what lies beyond. For that we need to take a creative leap to complete the bootstrap. Whatever new theory we construct, if we project it into the domain of current theories then it must there agree with current theories, or explain the discrepancy. So current theories cannot tell us what theory is next, but can provide feedback on candidates we propose.

This may sound abstract. But it has personal import. Each of us, in our brief window of life, faces personal questions. Who am I? Why am I? Our answers matter for how we live, find personal meaning, and face our own death. But any answer we give ourselves is a theory—perhaps less sophisticated than a scientific theory, perhaps not. So any answer we create has limits, and cannot be the final answer. I can give no final true theory of who I am and why I am. Some concepts may offer helpful perspectives; none yields a final answer. But in this case I have a unique situation, not found in other domains of science: although no theory of myself is the truth, I am myself. I can choose to watch myself, observe myself, be myself, in a silence devoid of a veil of concepts. Being myself, being aware of being myself, as opposed to just thinking about myself, may lead to new conceptual insights about myself. But I will always transcend those concepts. Self-exploration is, in principle, infinite.

So it’s a good thing that job security in science is also infinite.
